title: "def" creates a function, which is executed when called.
when_to_show: When distinguishing between function definitions and function calls
body: "def" is a keyword used to define a function. Defining a function means creating a named block of code.
detail: It’s important to note that just because you encounter a `def` line doesn’t mean the code inside the function is executed immediately. The code inside a function is executed when the function is called by adding parentheses after the function name. For example, even if there is a `print('hi')` line below `def hello()`, nothing will be printed to the screen unless you call `hello()`.

title: The `return` statement returns a value to the outside of the function.
when_to_show: When the result of a function is stored in a variable or used in another calculation
body: "return" is a keyword that returns the result calculated by a function to the outside of the function.
detail: While "print" displays a value on the screen, "return" sends the value back to the point where the function was called. For example, in `result = add(2, 3)`, when the `add` function executes `return 5`, the entire call `add(2, 3)` is replaced with `5`, and that value is stored in `result`. You can store the return value in a variable, compare it, or reuse it as input for another function.

title: A "parameter" is a placeholder, while an "argument" is the actual value entered.
when_to_show: When distinguishing between the name inside the function parentheses and the value passed when calling the function
body: "Parameter" and "argument" are terms that are often confused in the context of functions.
detail: A parameter is the name written inside the parentheses when defining a function, while an argument is the value actually passed when calling the function. For example, in `def greet(name):`, `name` is the parameter, and in `greet('Mina')`, `'Mina'` is the argument. When a function is executed, the argument value is used within the function as if it were assigned to the parameter name.

title: "print" and "return" handle results in different ways.
when_to_show: When distinguishing whether a function only outputs something or returns a value
body: Although `print` and `return` both deal with values that appear to be results, they serve different purposes.
detail: `print` is a function that displays the current value on the screen, while `return` is a keyword that returns the function’s result to the point where it was called. If you execute `print('hi')` inside a function, “hi” will appear on the screen, but that does not necessarily mean the function returned a value. If you store the result of a function call that lacks a `return` statement in a variable, it usually contains `None`.

title: Variables inside a function are temporary labels used during the function's execution.
when_to_show: When checking how far a variable created within a function is used
body: Variables inside a function can be thought of as temporary labels used during the function’s execution.
detail: Since this card serves as a reference for explaining the structure of local variables, it provides a basic model that should be the first thing to come to mind when solving scope-related problems. For example, if you define `total = a + b` inside `def add(a, b):`, `total` is a name that makes the calculation within the function easier to read. While there may be a variable named `total` outside the function, the `total` that is newly assigned inside the function does not always modify the `total` outside the function.

title: Functions allow you to reuse the same rule for multiple values.
when_to_show: When reading a flow where the same function is called multiple times
body: A major advantage of functions is that the same rule can be reused for multiple values. Once you define a rule using `def`, you can call it multiple times with different arguments.
detail: For example, `double(3)` returns 6, and `double(5)` returns 10. Although the code inside the function is the same, the result changes because the values passed as parameters are different. When reading code, if the same function name appears multiple times, it’s a good idea to write down the argument values for each call separately.

title: When a `return` statement is encountered, the function execution ends at that point.
when_to_show: When determining whether the code following the `return` statement is executed
body: The `return` statement returns a value and also terminates the execution of the function.
detail: When a `return` statement is encountered within a function, any code that remains in the same indented block below it is not executed. For example, even if there is a `print('after')` on the line following `return 'ok'`, `after` will not be printed if the `return` statement is executed first. When a `return` statement appears inside a conditional statement, you must verify under what conditions the function terminates early.

title: A function is defined by its input, processing, and output.
when_to_show: When you need to quickly understand the overall purpose of a function
body: Functions are easier to understand if you think of them as a set of conventions regarding input, processing, and output.
detail: Input consists of parameters and arguments; processing is the block of code inside the function; and output is either a return value or screen output. Function names are usually chosen to briefly describe this agreement. For example, `count_items` is likely a function that counts items, and `normalize_name` is likely a function that formats names.
